resources.string: Needs your explicit approval before an app can use it.
Only apps signed with the same key as the app that declared it can hold this.
Reserved for the system and granted by internal rules rather than by you.
Usually granted automatically at install. Low risk on its own.
%1$s uses SHA-256 or a stronger digest. No practical collision attack is known, though overall security also depends on the signing key type and size.
%1$s uses SHA-1. SHA-1 is no longer collision resistant, so an attacker can create different data with the same digest. New signing certificates should use SHA-256 or stronger.
%1$s uses MD5. MD5 is not collision resistant and is unsafe for signing certificates. New signing certificates should use SHA-256 or stronger.
%1$s uses MD2. MD2 is obsolete and vulnerable to practical attacks, so it is unsafe for signing certificates. New signing certificates should use SHA-256 or stronger.
The strength of %1$s cannot be assessed from its algorithm name. Key type and size may also affect its security.
